title: No rational soul is a worm
source_text: Εἰ δὲ τὴν τοῦ ἀνθρώπου μικρότητα οὐ διὰ τὸ σῶμα ἐξευτελίζετε ἀλλὰ διὰ τὴν ψυχὴν, ὡς οὖσαν ὑποδεεστέραν τῶν λοιπῶν λογικῶν καὶ μάλιστα σπουδαίων καὶ διὰ τοῦθ᾿ ὑποδεεστέραν, ἐπείπερ ἡ κακία ἐστίν ἐν αὐτῇ, τί μᾶλλον οἱ ἐν Χριστιανοῖς φαῦλοι καὶ οἱ ἐν Ἰουδαίοις κακῶς βιοῦντες ὁρμαθός εἰσι νυκτερίδων ἢ μύρμηκες ἢ σκώληκες ἢ βάτραχοι, ἢ οἱ ἐν τοῖς λοιποῖς ἔθνεσι μοχθηροί; ὡς κατὰ τοῦτο πάνθ᾿ ὁντιναοῦν, μάλιστα κεχυμένῃ τῇ κακίᾳ χρώμενον, νυκτερίδα καὶ σκώληκα καὶ βάτραχον καὶ μύρμηκα εἶναι ὡς πρὸς τοὺς λοιποὺς ἀνθρώπους. κἂν Δημοσθένης τις οὖν ὁ ῥήτωρ ᾖ μετὰ τῆς παραπλησίας ἐκείνῳ κακίας καὶ τῶν ἀπὸ κακίας αὐτῷ πεπραγμένων, κἂν Ἀντιφῶν ἄλλος ῥήτωρ νομιζόμενος εἶναι, καὶ τὴν πρόνοιαν ἀναιρῶν ἐν τοῖς ἐπιγεγραμμένοις περὶ ἀληθείας παραπλησίως τῇ Κέλσου ἐπιγραφῇ· οὐδὲν ἧττόν εἰσιν οὗτοι σκώληκες ἐν βορβόρου γωνίᾳ τοῦ τῆς ἀμαθίας καὶ ἀγνοίας καλινδούμενοι. καίτοι γε ὁποῖον δὴ τὸ λογικὸν οὐκ ἂν εὐλόγως σκώληκι παραβάλλοιτο, ἀφορμὰς ἔχον πρὸς ἀρετήν. αὗται γὰρ αἱ πρὸς αὐτὴν ὑποτυπώσεις οὐκ ἐῶσι σκώληκι παραβάλλεσθαι τοὺς δυνάμει ἔχοντας τὴν ἀρετὴν καὶ τὰ σπέρματα αὐτῆς πάντῃ ἀπολέσαι οὐ δυναμένους. οὐκοῦν ἀναφαίνεται ὅτι οὔθ᾿ οἱ ἄνθρωποι καθόλου σκώληκες ἂν εἶεν ὡς πρὸς θεόν· ὁ γὰρ λόγος τὴν ἀρχὴν ἔχων ἀπὸ τοῦ παρὰ θεοῦ λόγου οὐκ ἐᾷ τὸ λογικὸν ζῷον πάντῃ ἀλλότριον νο μισθῆναι θεοῦ· οὔτε μᾶλλον οἱ ἐν Χριστιανοῖς καὶ Ἰουδαίοις φαῦλοι. καὶ ὡς πρὸς τὸ ἀληθὲς οὐ Χριστιανοὶ οὐδὲ Ἰουδαῖοι. τῶν λοιπῶν φαύλων παραβάλλοιντο ἐν γωνίᾳ βορβόρου καλινδουμένοις σκώληξιν. εἰ δ᾿ ἡ τοῦ λόγου φύσις οὐδὲ τοῦτο παραδέξασθαι ἐπιτρέπει, δηλονότι οὐχ ὑβρίσομεν τὴν πρὸς ἀρετὴν κατεσκευασμένην ἀνθρωπίνην φύσιν, κἂν δι᾿ ἄγνοιαν ἐξαμαρτάνῃ. οὐδ᾿ ἐξομοιώσομεν αὐτὴν τοῖς τοιοῖσδε ζῴοις.
pass_a_gloss: But if the smallness of man you disparage (ἐξευτελίζω) not because of the body but because of the soul (ψυχή), as being inferior (ὑποδεεστέρα) to the remaining rational ones (λογικά) and especially the virtuous (σπουδαῖοι), and inferior for this reason, since wickedness (κακία) is in it, why rather (τί μᾶλλον) are the base (φαῦλοι) among Christians and those living badly (κακῶς βιοῦντες) among Jews a cluster of bats or ants or worms or frogs, than the wicked (μοχθηροί) among the remaining nations (ἔθνη)? So that according to this anyone whatsoever (ὁντιναοῦν), especially one using poured-out/unrestrained (κεχυμένη) wickedness, is a bat and worm and frog and ant as in relation to the rest of men. And even if someone is Demosthenes the orator (ῥήτωρ), with wickedness closely like his and the things done by him from wickedness, and even if Antiphon, another reckoned (νομίζω) to be an orator, also abolishing (ἀναιρέω) providence (πρόνοια) in the [books] entitled (ἐπιγράφω) 'On Truth' (περὶ ἀληθείας), closely like the title (ἐπιγραφή) of Celsus: none the less these are worms rolling (καλινδέομαι) in a corner of the mire of stupidity/folly (ἀμαθία) and ignorance (ἄγνοια). And yet a rational being of whatever sort (ὁποῖον δή) would not reasonably (εὐλόγως) be compared to a worm, having starting points/resources (ἀφορμαί) toward virtue (ἀρετή). For these outlines/rudiments (ὑποτυπώσεις) toward it do not allow (ἐάω) those having virtue in potential (δυνάμει) and not able to lose/destroy (ἀπόλλυμι) its seeds (σπέρματα) wholly (πάντῃ) to be compared to a worm. Therefore it appears (ἀναφαίνεται) that neither would men in general (καθόλου) be worms in relation to God; for reason (λόγος), having its beginning (ἀρχή) from the Word/Reason that is from God (ὁ παρὰ θεοῦ λόγος, παρά + genitive), does not allow the rational animal (λογικὸν ζῷον) to be thought (νομίζω) wholly alien (ἀλλότριον) to God; nor rather the base among Christians and Jews, and who in relation to truth are not Christians nor Jews, than the remaining base, would be compared to worms rolling in a corner of mire. And if the nature (φύσις) of reason does not permit (ἐπιτρέπω) accepting (παραδέχομαι) even this, clearly we shall not insult (ὑβρίζω) the human nature (ἀνθρωπίνη φύσις) constructed/made (κατασκευάζω) for virtue, even if through ignorance it sins (ἐξαμαρτάνω), nor shall we liken (ἐξομοιόω) it to such animals.
pass_b_english: But suppose you scorn man’s littleness not because of the body but because of the soul, on the ground that it is inferior to the other rational beings, and especially to the virtuous ones, and inferior for this reason, that wickedness is in it. Why, then, are the bad among Christians and those among Jews who live evil lives any more a cluster of bats, or ants, or worms, or frogs, than the wicked among the other nations? On this reckoning anyone at all, and above all one given over to unrestrained wickedness, is a bat and a worm and a frog and an ant compared with the rest of humankind.

So even if a man is Demosthenes the orator, with wickedness like his and the deeds he did out of wickedness, or Antiphon, who is also reckoned an orator and who denied providence in the books entitled On Truth, a title like that of Celsus, none the less these men are worms rolling about in a corner of the mire of folly and ignorance.

And yet no rational being of any kind whatever could reasonably be compared to a worm, since it has starting points for virtue. For these first sketches of virtue do not allow those who have virtue in potential, and who cannot wholly lose its seeds, to be compared to a worm. It appears, then, that human beings in general could not be worms in relation to God, for reason, which takes its beginning from the Word who comes from God, does not allow the rational living being to be thought wholly alien to God. Nor could the bad among Christians and Jews, who in truth are neither Christians nor Jews, be compared to worms rolling about in a corner of the mire any more than the other bad.

And if the nature of reason does not allow us to accept even this, then plainly we shall not insult human nature, which was made for virtue, even if it sins through ignorance, nor shall we liken it to such animals.

choices.choice: 'Word who is with God' corrected to 'Word who comes from God' (παρὰ θεοῦ + genitive = from God); Pass A gloss and note fixed to match
'Why ... should ... be' changed to 'Why ... are' (indicative εἰσι, no modality)
'could not be worms' for potential ἂν εἶεν (was 'cannot')
φαῦλοι now 'the bad' and μοχθηροί 'the wicked', keeping the two words distinct
'belittle the littleness' rephrased 'scorn man's littleness ... on the ground that it is inferior'
'For' added for γάρ before 'these first sketches'
'the corner of the mire' to 'a corner of the mire' (anarthrous)

The opening conditional ('Εἰ δὲ ... ἐξευτελίζετε') is rendered 'But suppose you scorn' and the apodosis as the question 'Why, then...'; 'τί μᾶλλον ... εἰσι' is indicative and rendered 'why ... are ... any more', not 'should'. φαῦλοι (the morally bad, the Stoic opposite of σπουδαῖοι) is rendered 'the bad' throughout, and μοχθηροί 'the wicked', to keep the two Greek words distinct. 'κεχυμένῃ τῇ κακίᾳ χρώμενον' rendered 'given over to unrestrained wickedness'. Origen's charge of wickedness against Demosthenes is his own and is kept; 'μετὰ τῆς παραπλησίας ἐκείνῳ κακίας' is ambiguous in the Greek and the English 'with wickedness like his' keeps that ambiguity. Antiphon is the sophist whose work 'On Truth' (Περὶ ἀληθείας) Origen likens in title to Celsus's 'True Doctrine' (Ἀληθὴς λόγος); the title is given in English without quotation marks or italics. ἀναιρῶν rendered 'denied'. ἀμαθία rendered 'folly'. ἀφορμαί rendered 'starting points', ὑποτυπώσεις 'first sketches', δυνάμει 'in potential'; ἀπολέσαι rendered 'lose', since the point is that the seeds cannot be wholly lost. 'ἂν εἶεν' is potential and rendered 'could not be'. 'ὁ λόγος τὴν ἀρχὴν ἔχων ἀπὸ τοῦ παρὰ θεοῦ λόγου': the first λόγος is human reason, the second the divine Word, capitalised; 'παρὰ θεοῦ' (παρά with the genitive) means 'from God' and is rendered 'who comes from God'. This may recall John 1:1 or John 1:9, but the wording differs, so it is not cited inline. The source splits 'νο μισθῆναι' (νομισθῆναι) across a line break; read as one word. The clause 'οὔτε μᾶλλον οἱ ἐν Χριστιανοῖς καὶ Ἰουδαίοις φαῦλοι ... τῶν λοιπῶν φαύλων παραβάλλοιντο' is the second limb of 'οὔθ᾿ ... οὔτε' and is given its own sentence in English. 'κἂν δι᾿ ἄγνοιαν ἐξαμαρτάνῃ' kept as concessive ('even if it sins through ignorance'). No Scripture quoted.
